opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I've been thinking about for a long time, and I don't think there's a single answer. A few factors seem to matter.

The first is frequency, and especially the frequency of the *diagnostic* evidence. Take subject-verb agreement. Most sentences where the verb agrees with its subject are trivially easy: the subject is right next to the verb. The hard cases are when there's an intervening noun with a different number, like "the key to the cabinets *is* on the table." Those "attractor" configurations are rare in natural text. So a model can get very good at agreement overall while getting very little direct signal about what happens when a surface heuristic, like "agree with the most recent noun," gives the wrong answer. A lot of what makes a phenomenon hard is how often the data actually distinguishes the right generalization from a shallower one that works most of the time.

The second is the gap between surface statistics and the underlying structure. Some phenomena can be approximated well with linear, local, n-gram-ish cues. Others really depend on hierarchical structure, like long-distance dependencies, filler-gap constructions, island constraints, or the scope of negation and quantifiers. Even when models have enough data, there's a question of whether their inductive biases favor the hierarchical generalization or the linear one. In our work on things like question formation, where the classic poverty-of-the-stimulus argument comes from, we found that architectures without an explicit bias toward hierarchy often generalize linearly when the training data is ambiguous between the two. That's revealing about what the model brings to the table, separate from the data.

Third, some phenomena are hard because they're about the *absence* of something. Island constraints are a good example. The evidence that you can't extract from certain structures is mostly negative: those sentences just don't occur. A learner has to infer from their absence that they're ungrammatical rather than merely rare. That's a hard inference for any learner, human or machine, and models trained on next-word prediction don't obviously have a principled way of making it.

And then there's a more methodological point. "Hard for the model" isn't a single thing. A model can assign higher probability to the grammatical sentence in a minimal pair and still be relying on heuristics that break down on slightly different inputs. So I try to separate whether a model gets the phenomenon right on a benchmark from whether it has learned the generalization we think humans have. Those can come apart, and the interesting cases are usually where they do.

So my general framing is that difficulty comes from how much the training data underdetermines the right generalization, combined with how well the learner's inductive biases fill that gap. Comparing that to the human case, where children seem to arrive at the hierarchical generalization from far less data, is one of the things that makes this question exciting to me.

r001.rationale: It says diagnostic configurations are rare in natural text and that limited evidence makes the correct generalization harder to learn.

r002.rationale: It compares models’ learning with children’s ability to reach hierarchical generalizations from far less data.

r003.rationale: It discusses different phenomena and the limits of benchmark results, but does not state that broader testing found uneven model success across phenomena.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I've come to think about it is that there isn't really a single axis of "hard" here. There are at least two or three things going on that get conflated.

The first is just frequency. Language models are, at the end of the day, statistical learners, and if a construction shows up often enough in the training data, they'll pick it up, more or less regardless of how structurally complex a linguist would say it is. So a lot of what looks like a hard phenomenon turns out to be a rare phenomenon. And conversely, things that we'd think of as deeply compositional, like subject-verb agreement, work pretty well in the easy cases because there's just an enormous amount of evidence for them.

The second thing, which I find more interesting, is what happens when the surface statistics and the actual structure come apart. Agreement is my favorite example here because of the agreement attraction work, which has a long history in psycholinguistics. If you have a sentence like "the keys to the cabinet are on the table," the verb has to agree with "keys," not "cabinet," but "cabinet" is right there, it's the most recent noun. A model that's relying on a heuristic like "agree with the nearest noun" will get the common cases right and fail precisely on these. And what we found, early on with LSTMs and later with transformers, is that models do get these wrong at rates that are way above what you'd see from a system that had actually induced the hierarchical rule. They look like they've learned syntax until you probe the cases where the linear cue and the hierarchical cue disagree.

So one way to say it is: a phenomenon is hard to the extent that there's a shallower generalization that covers most of the training data. The model has no particular pressure to find the deeper rule if the shallow one gets it ninety-five percent of the way there. Humans, for whatever reason, seem to arrive at the hierarchical generalization even from relatively little data, and that's exactly where the inductive bias question comes in. Kids aren't getting more data than GPT, they're getting dramatically less, so the difference has to be in what the learner brings to the problem.

And then the third factor, which is a little more mundane but matters a lot, is dependency length and interference. Long-distance dependencies are harder, and especially long-distance dependencies with intervening material that's similar to the thing you need to track. That's true for humans too, actually, which is part of why I think the comparison is so productive. Some of the errors models make look remarkably human, and some of them look nothing like human errors at all, and both of those outcomes tell you something.

I'd add one caveat, which is that as models have scaled up, a lot of the specific benchmark items that used to break them don't anymore. That's real progress, but I'm a bit wary of reading it as "the model learned the rule." Often the right follow-up question is whether it learned it in a way that generalizes to constructions that are genuinely rare in the training distribution, or whether we've just moved the failure further out into the tail. The methodology that I think still holds up is to find cases where the plausible shallow heuristic and the real structural generalization make different predictions, and go test those specifically, rather than aggregate accuracy on a mix of easy and hard items.

r001.rationale: The response says that constructions appearing rarely in training data can be hard for models to learn, while frequent constructions are more likely to be learned.

r002.rationale: It contrasts children’s dramatically smaller amount of data with GPT’s and says the difference points to what the learner brings to the problem.

r003.rationale: It describes models succeeding on common or easy cases but failing on agreement-attraction cases and long-distance dependencies, with benchmark performance changing as models scale.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different things that we might mean by “harder.” One is that a phenomenon requires a more complex computation. Another is that the evidence you need to learn it is rare. And those don’t necessarily go together. Something can be quite simple once you’ve figured out the rule, but difficult to learn because you don’t often see examples that distinguish that rule from a simpler shortcut.

Subject–verb agreement is a useful example. If you have “the key to the cabinets is on the table,” the verb agrees with “key,” even though “cabinets” is closer. In many ordinary sentences, agreeing with the closest noun gives you the right answer. So a model can do pretty well without learning which noun actually controls agreement. You need particular kinds of examples to tell those possibilities apart.

So I’d want to look at both the distribution of the training data and the model’s inductive biases—what kinds of generalizations its architecture makes easier to learn. And I’d distinguish getting high accuracy on typical sentences from reliably generalizing to cases where the usual shortcuts don’t work. That second question is often where you discover what was difficult about learning the phenomenon.

r001.rationale: It says a phenomenon can be hard to learn because the evidence is rare and distinguishing examples are not often seen.

r002.rationale: It discusses how much evidence models need, but does not compare that amount with how few examples humans need.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes typical-sentence accuracy from reliable generalization, but does not state that broader testing found uneven success across linguistic phenomena.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of things that can make a phenomenon hard, and it’s useful to distinguish them. One is just how much relevant evidence there is in the training data. Something might look like a complicated grammatical rule to us, but if there are lots of examples of it, a model might learn it quite easily. And conversely, something that seems simple might be difficult if the evidence is rare or indirect.

The other part is what kind of generalization the model needs to make. Take subject–verb agreement. If the subject is right next to the verb, you can often get the right answer using a fairly superficial strategy. But if there are other nouns in between, then you need to figure out which noun is actually the subject. So the question becomes whether the model has learned that structural relationship or whether it’s relying on cues that usually work but fail in particular cases.

That’s why I think controlled experiments are important. If you just look at average performance on naturally occurring sentences, you can miss the distinction between learning a general rule and learning a collection of useful shortcuts. You want to vary things like distance, intervening nouns, and how frequent the construction is, and see which of those actually causes difficulty.

r001.rationale: It says a phenomenon can be difficult when relevant training evidence is rare or indirect.

r002.rationale: It does not compare how many examples models need with how few examples humans need.

r003.rationale: It discusses possible differences in difficulty, but does not state that broader testing found uneven success across linguistic phenomena.
